questions.stem: Sophia, 20, with known asthma, is in ED speaking 3 to 4 words at a time. Oxygen and salbutamol have been started and you have time for only a few targeted questions about her asthma history. Which question best identifies her risk of a fatal asthma attack?
options: How old were you when you were first diagnosed with asthma?
Does anyone else in your family have asthma, eczema or hay fever?
Have you ever needed intensive care or a breathing tube for asthma?
What do you think set off this attack while you were jogging in the cold this morning?
questions.why: A previous ICU admission or intubation for asthma is the strongest predictor of a future fatal attack. Always ask about it, along with hospital admissions, courses of oral steroids, current control and whether she uses a preventer.
notes: Age at diagnosis has little bearing on how dangerous an acute attack is, and asking about it wastes her limited breath.
Family atopy supports the diagnosis of asthma but does not tell you how likely this attack is to be fatal.
Knowing the trigger helps later education, but it does not stratify her risk of dying from this attack.

questions.stem: Sophia, 20, has severe acute asthma in ED: she speaks 3 to 4 words per breath, is using her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 92% on room air. She can use a spacer, and oxygen titrated to 93 to 95% has been started. Which salbutamol regimen should you prescribe for the first hour?
options: 12 puffs (100 microgram) by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes
4 puffs by pMDI and spacer every 4 minutes until help arrives
2.5 mg by nebuliser every 4 hours, with puffs as needed between
IV salbutamol infusion as the first-line bronchodilator
questions.why: For severe acute asthma in adults, the Australian Asthma Handbook recommends salbutamol 12 puffs by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or 5 mg by nebuliser if she cannot use a spacer. Give ipratropium and oral prednisolone with it.
notes: This is the community asthma first aid plan for use until an ambulance arrives, not the regimen for severe asthma in ED.
This dose is far too small and too infrequent for severe asthma, which needs repeated doses every 20 minutes in the first hour.
IV salbutamol is not first line. It is kept for refractory asthma under senior or ICU direction, because inhaled salbutamol works as well with fewer adverse effects.

questions.stem: Sophia's arrival ABG, taken on oxygen, showed pH 7.51 and pCO2 28 mmHg. One hour later she is still very breathless and wheezy despite treatment, and a repeat gas shows a pCO2 of 44 mmHg. What does this rise in pCO2 most likely reflect?
options: Renal bicarbonate retention correcting the earlier alkalaemia
Respiratory muscle fatigue with falling alveolar ventilation
Bronchospasm easing, so her ventilation has returned to normal
Loss of hypoxic respiratory drive caused by the extra oxygen
questions.why: Early in acute asthma, hyperventilation drives the pCO2 down. If the pCO2 climbs back to normal while she is still distressed, she is tiring and her alveolar ventilation is failing. This is a sign of life-threatening asthma and needs senior and ICU review.
notes: Renal compensation takes days, and it changes bicarbonate, not pCO2. It would not raise the pCO2 within an hour.
If she were improving, her distress and wheeze would be settling. A 'normal' pCO2 in a patient who is still struggling to breathe is ominous.
Hypercapnia from oxygen happens in chronic CO2 retainers such as some people with COPD, not in a young woman with acute asthma who was hypocapnic on arrival.

questions.stem: Sophia is sitting bolt upright, leaning forward with her hands braced on her knees (tripod position). Bracing her arms fixes her shoulder girdle. Which muscles does this position let her recruit most effectively as accessory muscles of inspiration?
questions.why: When the arms and scapulae are fixed, the pectoral muscles reverse their usual action. Instead of moving the arm, they pull on the ribs and sternum and lift the chest wall. This is why breathless patients brace their arms in the tripod position.
notes: These are the primary muscles of inspiration. They work whatever the arm position, so they are not the accessory muscles this posture recruits.
These are muscles of forced expiration, not inspiration.
These muscles mainly elevate and rotate the scapula. They have no useful attachment to the ribs for expanding the chest.
